topic: Why Nepal is stranger than you think, starting at the Sunauli border
hook: Your rickshaw ride at Sunauli takes you into a country where the year is 2083.
title: Nepal: 15 Minutes Ahead and Already in 2083
description:
Walk across the open India-Nepal border at Sunauli and you enter a country with its own clock, its own year, a flag that is not a rectangle and a child worshipped as a living goddess. This video covers six true facts about Nepal that sound made up, from the 45-minute time zone to how Mount Everest was measured by two countries. Stay to the end for the strangest one.

#Nepal #StrangeFacts #Geography
comment_prompt: Which Nepal fact surprised you most?

chapters.title: A border you can walk across
The flag that is not a rectangle

scenes.narration: Your rickshaw ride at Sunauli takes you into a country where the year is 2083.
scenes.headline: Cross On Foot

scenes.narration: No visa. No passport stamp. Just a plain gate, a few rickshaws, and suddenly you are standing in a different country.
scenes.headline: No Visa Needed

scenes.narration: And that is only the first strange thing. Nepal runs a clock fifteen minutes off from yours, and flies a flag that breaks a world rule.
scenes.headline: Odd Clock, Odd Flag

scenes.narration: By the end you will see how Mount Everest was measured twice, and why a small child is worshipped as a living goddess.
scenes.headline: Coming Up

scenes.narration: Stay for the last one. It happens in a capital city that is only a short flight from Delhi.
scenes.headline: Save The Best

scenes.narration: But let us start where you stand, at the border town of Sunauli in Uttar Pradesh, a few hours from Gorakhpur.
scenes.headline: Start At Sunauli

scenes.narration: One: a border you can simply walk across.
scenes.headline: An Open Border

scenes.narration: Walk a few minutes north from Sunauli and you reach Belahiya, in Nepal. The next big town beyond it is Bhairahawa.
scenes.headline: Sunauli To Belahiya

scenes.narration: There is a gate, a sign, and a line of rickshaws. There is no wall of visa counters and no queue for a stamp.
scenes.headline: Just A Simple Gate

scenes.narration: From there, buses run on to Kathmandu and Pokhara, so many travellers begin their whole Nepal trip right on this road.
scenes.headline: Next Stop Kathmandu

scenes.narration: The reason is an old treaty. In 1950, India and Nepal signed a friendship treaty that keeps the border open for their citizens.
scenes.headline: The 1950 Treaty

scenes.narration: Under it, Indians and Nepalis can travel, live and work across the line with a freedom that most countries never give each other.
scenes.headline: Live And Work

scenes.narration: You should still carry a valid ID, and vehicles have their own paperwork. But you never apply for a visa.
scenes.headline: Carry Your ID

scenes.narration: Many Nepali citizens even serve in the Indian Army, in Gorkha regiments that have stood on our side for generations.
scenes.headline: Gorkha Regiments

scenes.narration: Money is tied together too. Nepal fixes its rupee to ours: one hundred Indian rupees equal one hundred sixty Nepali rupees.
scenes.headline: Linked Rupees

scenes.narration: And a short drive from this gate is Lumbini, where the Buddha was born. Many people cross at Sunauli just for that.
scenes.headline: Birthplace Of Buddha

scenes.narration: So you crossed a country line without a visa. Now watch what happens to your watch.
scenes.headline: Check Your Watch

scenes.narration: Two: the clock that is fifteen minutes off.
scenes.headline: The 15-Minute Clock

scenes.narration: India runs on one time zone, five hours thirty minutes ahead of world time. Walk into Nepal and it becomes five forty-five.
scenes.headline: UTC +5:45

scenes.narration: So if your phone follows the local network, it jumps fifteen minutes ahead. Same sun, same sky, a different minute.
scenes.headline: Phone Jumps Ahead

scenes.narration: Look at that number. A time ending in forty-five is almost unheard of anywhere else on Earth.
scenes.headline: Why Forty-Five?

scenes.narration: Nepal is the only country in the world that uses this offset for its whole territory.
scenes.headline: Only Nepal

scenes.narration: The reason is a choice Nepal made for itself: a time tied to a line of longitude that runs through its own mountains.
scenes.headline: Its Own Meridian

scenes.narration: In other words, Nepal wanted its own clock, even if it sits only a quarter of an hour away from ours.
scenes.headline: Own Clock

scenes.narration: So when it is noon in Sunauli, it is already twelve fifteen a few minutes away in Belahiya.
scenes.headline: Noon Becomes 12:15

scenes.narration: A quarter of an hour sounds small. But the next thing is bigger: Nepal is living in a different year.
scenes.headline: A Different Year

scenes.narration: Three: a country that lives in the future.
scenes.headline: The Year Is 2083

scenes.narration: Look at an official Nepali calendar today and it does not say 2026. It says 2083.
scenes.headline: Not 2026

scenes.narration: That is Bikram Sambat, Nepal's official calendar, and it runs more than fifty-six years ahead of the one on your phone.
scenes.headline: 56 Years Ahead

scenes.narration: It is a very old calendar, also known in parts of India, and Nepal uses it for government work and official dates.
scenes.headline: Official Calendar

scenes.narration: Its months have names like Baisakh and Jestha, which will sound familiar to anyone who knows the traditional Indian calendars.
scenes.headline: Baisakh, Jestha

scenes.narration: The new year does not begin in January. It begins in mid-April, around the time of Baisakhi.
scenes.headline: April New Year

scenes.narration: So a Nepali friend might say, I was born in twenty sixty. In your calendar, that is about two thousand three.
scenes.headline: Born In 2060?

scenes.narration: The week is different too. Offices in Nepal usually work Sunday to Friday, and Saturday is the main day off.
scenes.headline: Saturday Is Off

scenes.narration: Cross the gate on a Saturday and many offices on the Nepal side are shut, while the Indian side is open.
scenes.headline: Closed On Saturday

scenes.narration: A different year, a different weekend, a different clock. Now look up at what is flying above the buildings.
scenes.headline: Look Up

scenes.narration: Four: the only flag in the world that is not a rectangle.
scenes.headline: A Flag Like No Other

scenes.narration: Every other national flag is a rectangle or a square. Nepal's is the only one that is neither.
scenes.headline: Not A Rectangle

scenes.narration: It is two triangles stacked on top of each other, crimson red with a blue border, and a moon and a sun inside.
scenes.headline: Two Triangles

scenes.narration: Many people explain the two triangles as two Himalayan peaks, or as the two major religions, Hinduism and Buddhism.
scenes.headline: Peaks Or Religions

scenes.narration: The moon and the sun stand for the hope that Nepal will last as long as they do.
scenes.headline: Sun And Moon

scenes.narration: Crimson is the national colour, and the rhododendron, the national flower, is red too. Nepal even has forests of them.
scenes.headline: The Red Flower

scenes.narration: The flag is so exact that Nepal's constitution gives step by step instructions. You could draw it with just a ruler and compass.
scenes.headline: Drawn With A Compass

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places and facts like these, subscribe now, because the next two are the ones I was saving.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: The next one is a mountain that two countries could not agree on.
scenes.headline: Two Countries, One Peak

scenes.narration: Five: the mountain that had to be measured twice.
scenes.headline: Everest, Measured Twice

scenes.narration: Mount Everest sits on the line between Nepal and China. Nepal calls it Sagarmatha. In Tibet, it is Chomolungma.
scenes.headline: Three Names

scenes.narration: For years the two countries gave different heights. Nepal said eight thousand eight hundred forty-eight metres. China said about eight thousand eight hundred forty-four.
scenes.headline: Two Heights

scenes.narration: The gap came from the top. China counted the solid rock, while Nepal counted the snow and ice sitting over it.
scenes.headline: Rock Or Snow?

scenes.narration: In December 2020, both countries announced one shared number together: eight thousand eight hundred forty-eight point eight six metres.
scenes.headline: One Shared Number

scenes.narration: A Nepali survey team climbed to the top as part of that work, so Nepal had its own measurement from the summit.
scenes.headline: Nepali Surveyors

scenes.narration: And Everest is not alone. Nepal is home to eight of the world's fourteen peaks above eight thousand metres.
scenes.headline: Eight Giants

scenes.narration: Many climbers begin at Lukla, a tiny airport on a cliff, famous for a short runway that slopes uphill.
scenes.headline: Lukla Airport

scenes.narration: Now think back to the gate at Sunauli. That land is low, flat farmland called the Terai, right beside Uttar Pradesh.
scenes.headline: The Flat Terai

scenes.narration: The same country holds that flat plain and the highest point on Earth. Travel north and hot fields give way to ice.
scenes.headline: Plains To Ice

scenes.narration: Big mountains are strange. But the strangest thing in Nepal is not a mountain. It is a child.
scenes.headline: Now, A Child

scenes.narration: Six: a little girl who is worshipped as a goddess.
scenes.headline: The Living Goddess

scenes.narration: In Kathmandu, a young girl called the Kumari is believed to hold the spirit of a goddess, and people truly worship her.
scenes.headline: Meet The Kumari

scenes.narration: She is chosen as a small child, from a particular Newar community, after priests check her for many signs of calm and perfection.
scenes.headline: Chosen As A Child

scenes.narration: She then lives in a special house called the Kumari Ghar, right beside Durbar Square in the middle of Kathmandu.
scenes.headline: The Kumari Ghar

scenes.narration: Visitors can sometimes see her at a carved window above the courtyard, but taking her photograph is not allowed.
scenes.headline: At The Window

scenes.narration: She leaves rarely, and tradition says she must be carried, so that her feet do not touch the ground outside.
scenes.headline: Feet Never Touch Ground

scenes.narration: Once a year, during the Indra Jatra festival, she is pulled through the streets in a chariot while crowds watch.
scenes.headline: The Chariot Festival

scenes.narration: Leaders have traditionally visited her for a blessing. A child sits in that seat of honour, in a modern capital.
scenes.headline: Leaders Seek Blessings

scenes.narration: When she grows up and reaches puberty, she is no longer the goddess, and a new child is chosen to take her place.
scenes.headline: A New Kumari

scenes.narration: Nepal's Supreme Court has even told the state to make sure the Kumari gets an education, like any other child.
scenes.headline: School For A Goddess

scenes.narration: Think about that: a child who is a goddess, in a capital only a short flight from Delhi.
scenes.headline: A Short Flight Away

scenes.narration: So that rickshaw at Sunauli carries you somewhere with a different clock, a different year, a different flag and a taller mountain.
scenes.headline: From One Gate

scenes.narration: And all of it begins at an open gate with no visa, a few minutes' walk from an Indian road.
scenes.headline: No Visa, No Wall

scenes.narration: Your rickshaw ride at Sunauli takes you into a country where the year is 2083, and now you know why.
scenes.headline: 2083, Explained

scenes.headline: Next: Japan
